blocks.html: Hold your nose and eat a jelly bean: you can tell it's sweet, but not which flavor. Most of what we call flavor is smell.

The tongue senses five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami (savory, from glutamates in foods like Parmesan, tomatoes, mushrooms, soy sauce and meat). Aroma is smelled through the back of the nose as you chew and supplies most of a food's flavor. Texture, temperature and chemical feelings such as chile heat and mint's cool also shape how food tastes.

Every taste can be sensed all over the tongue; the old "tongue map" with one taste per zone is a myth. And because aroma matters so much, food tastes flat when you have a cold, and cold food tastes less salty and sweet than the same food warm.

Common sources
rows: Sugar, honey, ripe fruit, caramelized onions
Salt, soy sauce, cheese, cured meats, olives
Coffee, dark chocolate, radicchio, beer, charred bits
Parmesan, tomatoes, mushrooms, soy sauce, anchovies, meat broths

blocks.title: Name the taste
blocks.q: The savory, mouth-filling taste of aged Parmesan and a long-simmered broth.
steps: That is the taste of glutamates.

blocks.html: Believing the tongue map. Every part of the tongue senses every taste.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Taste a spoon of plain broth. Add a pinch of salt and taste; add a squeeze of lemon and taste; add a little grated Parmesan and taste. Write what each changed.
  • Eat a jelly bean with your nose held, then let go.

blocks.html: Seasoning is not just salt and pepper. Cooks balance four levers: salt, acid, fat and heat.

Salt makes food taste more like itself and softens bitterness. Acid (lemon, vinegar, wine) brightens and cuts richness. Fat carries flavor and gives richness. Heat means both cooking (browning builds flavor) and spice (chile, black pepper, mustard). Season in layers: a little salt at each stage seasons food through; a final adjustment at the end.

items: Salt pasta water well; the pasta can only absorb seasoning while it cooks.
Salt meat ahead of time (even hours, refrigerated) so it seasons inside.
Finish rich dishes with a squeeze of acid.
Add finishing salt (flaky salt) at the table for crunch.

blocks.html: Many cooks season by weight in a professional kitchen. Salt at about 1% of a dish's total weight is a common starting point for soups and braises, then adjusted by taste; different salts measure very differently by the spoon, so grams are reliable.

blocks.title: Salt by weight
blocks.q: A pot of soup weighs 4,000 g. About how much salt at 1%?

blocks.html: Adding all the salt at the end. It sits on the surface, tastes harsh, and the inside stays bland.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Make a simple tomato sauce and divide it into four bowls. Season one with salt only, one with salt and a little vinegar, one with salt and butter, one with salt and chile. Taste and rank them.

blocks.html: Great cooks taste constantly. The recipe gets you close; tasting gets you there.

Taste with a clean spoon each time (never double-dip). Taste at each stage, and at the temperature it will be served. To fix: flat or dull → salt, then acid; too salty → more of the unsalted base, or serve with something unsalted; too sour → a little sweetness or fat; too sweet → acid or salt; too bitter → salt, fat or sweetness; too spicy → fat (dairy) or more base.

items: Keep a cup of clean tasting spoons at your station and a second cup for used ones.
Taste the components separately and then together on the plate.
Adjust in small steps; you can always add, not take away.
Cold food needs a little more seasoning than hot.

blocks.html: Taste is relative. A pinch of salt can make a sauce taste less bitter; a squeeze of lemon can make a soup taste saltier without more salt. Small changes, tasted each time, teach you how ingredients talk to each other.

blocks.title: Fix it
blocks.q: A cream sauce tastes heavy and flat, but salty enough.
steps: Salt is fine; it needs brightness to cut richness.
blocks.a: Add a little acid (lemon juice or wine).

blocks.html: Trying to fix too much salt with sugar. Sugar masks a little but doesn't remove salt; dilute with more unsalted base instead.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Ask someone to make a soup too salty, too sour, or too flat on purpose, without telling you which. Taste, name the problem, and fix it.

blocks.html: Herbs are leaves; spices are seeds, bark, roots and berries. Each has a time to go into the pot.

Hardy herbs (thyme, rosemary, bay, sage, oregano) can cook a long time; add them early. Tender herbs (basil, parsley, cilantro, chives, dill, tarragon, mint) lose flavor with heat; add them at the end or raw. Dried herbs are stronger by volume: about 1 part dried for 3 parts fresh. Whole spices keep longer than ground; toasting them in a dry pan or blooming them in hot oil releases their aroma. Aromatics (onion, garlic, celery, carrot, ginger) are the flavor base of most dishes.

head: Classic aromatic base
Ingredients
rows: Onion, carrot, celery, cooked slowly in olive oil
Thyme, bay leaf and parsley stems, tied

blocks.html: Many flavor compounds in spices dissolve in fat, not water, and escape into the air with heat. Toasting and blooming in oil draw them out; long boiling sends them away.

blocks.title: Fresh to dried
blocks.q: A recipe calls for 3 tablespoons of fresh oregano. How much dried?
steps: About 1 part dried for 3 parts fresh.

blocks.html: Adding basil at the start of a long sauce. Add a few leaves early if you like, and most of it at the end.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Toast whole cumin seeds in a dry pan until fragrant, grind half, and compare their smell with pre-ground cumin from the jar.
  • Make the same soup twice, adding parsley early in one and at the end in the other.

blocks.html: A strawberry in June and a strawberry in January are different foods. Restaurants that cook with the seasons build their menus around what is at its best.

Seasonal produce, picked ripe nearby, usually has the most flavor and the lowest price. In much of the United States: spring brings asparagus, peas, radishes, spring onions and rhubarb; summer, tomatoes, corn, zucchini, berries, stone fruit and herbs; fall, apples, pears, squash, mushrooms and root vegetables; winter, citrus, cabbages, kale, stored roots and potatoes. Seasons shift with climate and region.

items: Build menus around a few seasonal stars and change them as the season turns.
Preserve the glut: pickles, jams and frozen purées carry summer into winter.
Talk to growers and market vendors; they know what's coming next week.
Write menus with dishes that can swap one vegetable for another as availability changes.

blocks.html: Produce shipped long distances is often picked before it's ripe so it survives the trip. Ripened on the plant and eaten soon, it's sweeter and more aromatic.

blocks.title: In season?
blocks.q: In much of the U.S., which is most in season in October: asparagus, tomatoes, or winter squash?
steps: Asparagus is spring; tomatoes peak in summer; squash is harvested in fall.

blocks.html: Planning a winter menu around ripe tomatoes and fresh berries.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Visit a farmers market and list what's there. Plan a three-course menu using only those things.

blocks.html: A menu is a promise to guests and a work plan for the kitchen. A good one balances both.

Balance the menu: a range of cooking methods, colors, textures, richness and prices, and spread the work across the stations. Describe dishes honestly and clearly; name what a guest needs to know (allergens, raw items). Price from cost: a common method divides the cost of one portion by the target food-cost percent (menu price = portion cost ÷ food-cost %). Menu analysis sorts dishes by how popular and how profitable they are, to decide what to keep, change or drop.
